cim: Attorney Suspended for Fake AI Cases, Other Ethics Violations
cim_eredeti: Attorney Suspended for Fake AI Cases, Other Ethics Violations
szoveg_eredeti:
The Supreme Court of Ohio today indefinitely suspended a Cleveland attorney for being dishonest about citing four artificial intelligence “hallucinated” cases in a lawsuit against the city of Cleveland, and for other ethical violations.

In a unanimous per curiam opinion, the Supreme Court indefinitely suspended Arleesha Wilson, who owes more than $647,000 in judgments for neglecting client matters, providing incompetent representation, and making false statements to courts. The judgments include a $7,500 sanction from a federal district court for citing four cases that do not exist, which she admitted only under questioning by the trial judge.

The Cleveland Metropolitan Bar Association filed a complaint against Wilson with the Board of Professional Conduct in 2025 based on five client matters, including the representation of a couple in a dispute over a commercial roofing contract. The couple eventually won a $625,000 judgment against Wilson in a legal malpractice case, and she was ordered to pay more than $14,000 to the roofing company's attorney.

When recommending that Wilson be suspended, the board noted that at the time of her March 2026 disciplinary hearing, Wilson had not paid any of the court-ordered penalties.

Lawyer Misleads Court About AI Use In 2024, Wilson filed a lawsuit on behalf of a security services company against the city of Cleveland in Cuyahoga County Common Pleas Court. Because the case included federal and state claims, the case was transferred to the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Ohio.

In April 2025, the city asked the district court to dismiss the case. Wilson filed a brief opposing the city. About two weeks after her brief was filed, the city told the court that Wilson’s brief identified quoted language from opinions; however, that language was not in the opinions she cited. The city also indicated she cited four cases that did not exist.

The federal court gave Wilson until September 2025 to provide copies of the four specific cases the city claimed did not exist, or to file an explanation of why she was unable to provide them. The federal court noted it was unable to find the cases using standard legal research tools.

Wilson responded by submitting 1,395 pages of case law, which she claimed were copies of all the cases cited in her brief. The court responded that the four cases in question were not included in the attachment.

The court scheduled a hearing for Wilson to explain why she and her client should not be held in contempt of court for failing to provide the four cases. She was ordered to bring the four cases to the hearing. At the hearing, the trial judge confirmed that Wilson had not filed the cases with the court or explained why she was unable to do so.

During the contempt hearing, Wilson initially refused to admit that the four cases did not exist but instead submitted three other cases. The court noted that those cases were from different years and different courts, or had names slightly different from the cases at issue. The judge asked Wilson whether she had used AI to draft the opposition brief, and she confirmed she had. She then acknowledged she was unable to find the cases at issue.

The federal court declined to hold Wilson’s client in contempt for the submission but did rule that Wilson violated the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure by engaging in frivolous conduct. The court found she used the AI-hallucinated cases and also misrepresented the legal significance of seven other cases that were included in her brief.

In October 2025, the federal court ordered her to pay a $7,500 penalty within 30 days and to provide copies of the court’s order to her client, the Cleveland bar association, and the common pleas court. The case was then transferred back to common pleas court. Wilson agreed to make $250 monthly payments to the federal court, but at the time of her disciplinary hearing, she had not made a payment and had not provided a copy of the order against her to the common pleas court.

The board found that her conduct in the matter violated the rules against asserting an issue in a legal proceeding that is not supported by law, and from knowingly disobeying an obligation imposed by a court.

Attorney Inaction Prolongs Roofing Dispute Wilson was also charged with several professional conduct violations related to her representation of a couple who owned a commercial building that needed roof repairs.

The couple hired 1st Choice Roofing to do repairs, and the couple filed a breach of contract lawsuit against the roofers in November 2020. In July 2021, the trial court conducted a settlement conference with the parties, and Wilson told the court that the couple hired a new roofing contractor to replace the roof for $202,250. The court noted the price was far higher than the $95,000 the couple contracted to pay 1st Choice. The court told the parties to familiarize themselves with the case and that another settlement conference would be scheduled.

At the request of 1st Choice, Wilson was instructed to tell the couple to stop all work so that 1st Choice could inspect the roof before the new company installed a new roof. Although 1st Choice sent a cease and desist letter the same day as the court ordered all work to stop, the work continued, and the roof was completed before 1st Choice had a chance to inspect the building.

The couple stated under oath that they were unaware of 1st Choice’s request to stop the work or inspect the roof.

Wilson amended the complaint and refiled the lawsuit in February 2022. 1st Choice asked the court to dismiss the case, and Wilson failed to oppose the motion. The trial court dismissed all claims against 1st Choice made in the refiled case except for the breach of contract claim.

On the day of the trial, the judge learned that Wilson provided 1st Choice with copies of the new roofer’s contract and some photographs of the new roof, but did not provide any bills or invoices to explain the actual costs of the new roof. The trial court indicated that it was not inclined to hear the case and directed Wilson to provide the requested information to 1st Choice or risk having to pay the company’s legal fees.

The trial court eventually dismissed the couple’s case and ordered Wilson to pay 1st Choice’s attorney $13,155 for legal fees. When Wilson did not pay, the Court added $1,000 to the total owed.

The couple filed a malpractice case against Wilson, who did not answer the complaint. The court issued a default judgment against Wilson and awarded the couple $202,250 plus interest and costs. The court added $405,000 in punitive damages and ordered Wilson to pay $18,163 of the couple’s legal fees.

The board found Wilson’s rule violations in this case and others adversely reflect on her fitness to practice law.

The Court’s opinion noted that Wilson’s misconduct started in 2020, just two and a half years after she was admitted to practice law. At her disciplinary hearing, Wilson explained that she had heard concerns about a law firm having trouble getting people in the door, but did not understand that having too many clients could also be a problem. She stated she realized she “didn’t have the time to give proper care to every case.”

The opinion stated that while Wilson claims to have accepted accountability for her actions, “she has failed to comply with the payment plan that she proposed to the federal district court and has failed to make even one symbolic payment toward the more than $647,000 in restitution she has stipulated that she owes as a result of her misconduct.”

In addition to suspending Wilson, the Court ordered her to pay the costs of the disciplinary proceedings.

2026-0724. Cleveland Metro Bar Assn. v. Wilson, Slip Opinion No. 2026-Ohio-4626.
